claim: Fam20C is an atypical protein kinase uniquely localized to the secretory pathway lumen.
source: Our laboratory recently identified an atypical protein kinase, Fam20C, which is uniquely localized to the secretory pathway lumen.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known finding from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates calsequestrin2.
source: Here, we show that Fam20C phosphorylates several SR proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling, including calsequestrin2 and Stim1, whose biochemical activities are dramatically regulated by Fam20C mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays and cell-based phosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates Stim1.
source: Here, we show that Fam20C phosphorylates several SR proteins involved in Ca2+ signaling, including calsequestrin2 and Stim1, whose biochemical activities are dramatically regulated by Fam20C mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays and cell-based phosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phosphorylation of Stim1 by Fam20C enhances Stim1 activation and store-operated Ca2+ entry.
source: Notably, phosphorylation of Stim1 by Fam20C enhances Stim1 activation and store-operated Ca2+ entry.
evidence: Supported by crosslinking assays showing increased Stim1 activation with WT Fam20C compared to kinase-inactive mutant (Figure 2F,G).

claim: Mice with Fam20c ablated in cardiomyocytes develop heart failure following aging.
source: Physiologically, mice with Fam20c ablated in cardiomyocytes develop heart failure following either aging or induced pressure overload.
evidence: Demonstrated through echocardiography, hemodynamic measurements, and histological analysis in aged Fam20C cKO mice (Figures 3-6).

claim: Mice with Fam20c ablated in cardiomyocytes develop heart failure following induced pressure overload.
source: Physiologically, mice with Fam20c ablated in cardiomyocytes develop heart failure following either aging or induced pressure overload.
evidence: Demonstrated through TAC experiments showing exaggerated cardiac dysfunction in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 7).

claim: Non-muscle cells lacking Fam20C display altered ER Ca2+ signaling.
source: We extended these observations to show that non-muscle cells lacking Fam20C display altered ER Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through Ca2+ imaging and thapsigargin-induced ER Ca2+ release experiments in U2OS and HeLa cells (Figure 8).

claim: Fam20C plays an overarching role in ER/SR Ca2+ homeostasis and cardiac pathophysiology.
source: Overall, we show that Fam20C plays an overarching role in ER/SR Ca2+ homeostasis and cardiac pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective data from biochemical, cellular, and in vivo experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Heart failure remains the leading cause of death in the United States.
source: Heart failure remains the leading cause of death in the United States (Benjamin et al., 2018) and is clinically characterized by reduced cardiac function and pathological remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2018.

claim: Intracellular calcium handling is the basis of cardiac contraction and relaxation.
source: Intracellular calcium (Ca2+) handling is the basis of cardiac contraction and relaxation (Bers, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bers, 2014.

claim: Contraction involves the release of sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ into the cytosol via the ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2).
source: Contraction involves the release of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ into the cytosol via the ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2); relaxation occurs with SR Ca2+ uptake by the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase pump (SERCA2a) (Bers, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bers, 2002.

claim: Relaxation occurs with SR Ca2+ uptake by the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase pump (SERCA2a).
source: Contraction involves the release of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ into the cytosol via the ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2); relaxation occurs with SR Ca2+ uptake by the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase pump (SERCA2a) (Bers, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bers, 2002.

claim: Multiple proteins and post-translational modifications tightly regulate SR Ca2+ cycling, including phosphorylation of proteins on the cytosolic face of the SR.
source: Multiple proteins and post-translational modifications tightly regulate this SR Ca2+ cycling, including phosphorylation of proteins on the cytosolic face of the SR (Ai et al., 2005; Anderson et al., 2011; Chaanine and Hajjar, 2011), and are a focus of several clinical attempts to improve cardiac function (Marks, 2013; Hulot et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The biochemical and physiological roles of protein phosphorylation within the ER/SR remains essentially unknown.
source: Importantly, the biochemical and physiological roles of protein phosphorylation within the ER/SR remains essentially unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Fam20C has a signal peptide that brings it to the lumen of the secretory pathway.
source: The discovery of the atypical kinase Fam20C solved this conundrum, as Fam20C has a signal peptide that brings it to the lumen of the secretory pathway where it preferentially phosphorylates Ser within Ser-x-Glu/pSer (S-x-E) motifs (Tagliabracci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tagliabracci et al., 2012.

claim: Fam20C preferentially phosphorylates Ser within Ser-x-Glu/pSer (S-x-E) motifs.
source: The discovery of the atypical kinase Fam20C solved this conundrum, as Fam20C has a signal peptide that brings it to the lumen of the secretory pathway where it preferentially phosphorylates Ser within Ser-x-Glu/pSer (S-x-E) motifs (Tagliabracci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tagliabracci et al., 2012.

claim: Fam20C is important for bone and teeth formation in patients.
source: Fam20C is important for bone and teeth formation in patients (Simpson et al., 2007; Cui et al., 2015) and animal models (Vogel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2007 and Cui et al., 2015.

claim: Fam20C is important for bone and teeth formation in animal models.
source: Fam20C is important for bone and teeth formation in patients (Simpson et al., 2007; Cui et al., 2015) and animal models (Vogel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogel et al., 2012.

claim: Fam20C is responsible for generating >90% of the secreted phosphoproteome.
source: Subsequent studies demonstrated that Fam20C is responsible for generating >90% of the secreted phosphoproteome and that its substrates are likely involved in diverse biological functions that mostly remain uncharacterized (Tagliabracci et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tagliabracci et al., 2015.

claim: A heart disease-associated polymorphism in HRC (HRC-Ser96Ala) was observed within a Fam20C consensus S-x-E phosphorylation motif.
source: Fam20C's potential role in cardiac function was highlighted by the identification of a heart disease-associated polymorphism in luminal SR resident histidine-rich Ca2+-binding protein (HRC) (Arvanitis et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2013). Specifically, this polymorphism (HRC-Ser96Ala) was observed within a Fam20C consensus S-x-E phosphorylation motif and Fam20C was responsible for HRC-Ser96 phosphorylation (Pollak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arvanitis et al., 2008, Singh et al., 2013, and Pollak et al., 2017.

claim: Fam20C is responsible for HRC-Ser96 phosphorylation.
source: Specifically, this polymorphism (HRC-Ser96Ala) was observed within a Fam20C consensus S-x-E phosphorylation motif and Fam20C was responsible for HRC-Ser96 phosphorylation (Pollak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pollak et al., 2017.

claim: HRC-Ser96 phosphorylation modulated HRC's interactions with triadin and SERCA2a.
source: This phosphorylation modulated HRC's interactions with triadin and SERCA2a and was demonstrated to be necessary to prevent arrhythmias in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, implicitly from Pollak et al., 2017.

claim: HRC-Ser96 phosphorylation was demonstrated to be necessary to prevent arrhythmias in vitro.
source: This phosphorylation modulated HRC's interactions with triadin and SERCA2a and was demonstrated to be necessary to prevent arrhythmias in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work, implicitly from Pollak et al., 2017.

claim: Several SR Ca2+ regulatory proteins are Fam20C substrates.
source: Importantly, we hypothesize that several SR Ca2+ regulatory proteins are Fam20C substrates, given the extent of SR proteins containing S-x-E motifs and that Fam20C has been shown to be responsible for the majority of secretory pathway phosphorylation in several cell types (Tagliabracci et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on sequence motifs and prior findings about Fam20C's role in secretory pathway phosphorylation.

claim: Stim1 is important for controlling cellular Ca2+ content in many cell types.
source: Notably, we show that stromal interaction molecule 1 (Stim1), which is important for controlling cellular Ca2+ content in many cell types (Collins et al., 2013), and calsequestrin 2 (CSQ2), the major Ca2+ binding protein in the SR, are dramatically regulated by Fam20C phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2013.

claim: Calsequestrin 2 (CSQ2) is the major Ca2+ binding protein in the SR.
source: Notably, we show that stromal interaction molecule 1 (Stim1), which is important for controlling cellular Ca2+ content in many cell types (Collins et al., 2013), and calsequestrin 2 (CSQ2), the major Ca2+ binding protein in the SR, are dramatically regulated by Fam20C phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSQ2's function.

claim: Stim1 and CSQ2 are dramatically regulated by Fam20C phosphorylation.
source: Notably, we show that stromal interaction molecule 1 (Stim1), which is important for controlling cellular Ca2+ content in many cell types (Collins et al., 2013), and calsequestrin 2 (CSQ2), the major Ca2+ binding protein in the SR, are dramatically regulated by Fam20C phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Fam20C deficiency in cardiomyocytes results in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) upon numerous pathological stimuli.
source: Upon numerous pathological stimuli, we demonstrate that Fam20C deficiency in cardiomyocytes results in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).
evidence: This is demonstrated through aging, TAC, and isoproterenol experiments in Fam20C cKO mice (Figures 5-7).

claim: DCM involves left ventricle (LV) dilation and reduced functional capacity in both human and animal models.
source: DCM involves left ventricle (LV) dilation and reduced functional capacity in both human and animal models (Hershberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hershberger et al., 2013.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates triadin.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: Figure 1A shows autoradiograph demonstrating 32P incorporation into triadin when co-expressed with WT Fam20C but not kinase-inactive Fam20C.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates calumenin.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: Figure 1A shows autoradiograph demonstrating 32P incorporation into calumenin when co-expressed with WT Fam20C but not kinase-inactive Fam20C.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates calreticulin.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: Figure 1A shows autoradiograph demonstrating 32P incorporation into calreticulin when co-expressed with WT Fam20C but not kinase-inactive Fam20C.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates sarcalumenin.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: Figure 1A shows autoradiograph demonstrating 32P incorporation into sarcalumenin when co-expressed with WT Fam20C but not kinase-inactive Fam20C.

claim: CSQ2 has a single, conserved S-x-E site (Ser385) on its C-terminal tail.
source: It is intriguing that CSQ2 has a single, conserved S-x-E site (Ser385) on its C-terminal tail (Figure 1B), the region of the protein necessary for proper Ca2+ binding (Shin et al., 2000) and polymerization (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B with sequence alignment.

claim: The C-terminal tail of CSQ2 is the region of the protein necessary for proper Ca2+ binding.
source: It is intriguing that CSQ2 has a single, conserved S-x-E site (Ser385) on its C-terminal tail (Figure 1B), the region of the protein necessary for proper Ca2+ binding (Shin et al., 2000) and polymerization (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shin et al., 2000.

claim: The C-terminal tail of CSQ2 is the region of the protein necessary for polymerization.
source: It is intriguing that CSQ2 has a single, conserved S-x-E site (Ser385) on its C-terminal tail (Figure 1B), the region of the protein necessary for proper Ca2+ binding (Shin et al., 2000) and polymerization (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2003.

claim: Only WT CSQ2 was phosphorylated in H9C2 cells, not the Ser385Ala mutant.
source: Transfection of Flag-tagged WT and Ser385Ala mutant CSQ2 constructs into H9C2 rat myoblast cardiac cells, followed by 32P-orthophosphate labeling, revealed that only WT CSQ2 was phosphorylated (Figure 1C), suggesting that CSQ2-Ser385 is phosphorylated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by autoradiography in Figure 1C.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates CSQ2 only at Ser385.
source: Mutation of CSQ2 Ser385 to Ala abrogated phosphorylation, but mutation of Ser393 to Ala did not, suggesting that Fam20C phosphorylates CSQ2 only at Ser385.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Phosphorylated CSQ2 showed a greater propensity to form higher order polymeric structures than unphosphorylated CSQ2.
source: Indeed, we found that phosphorylated CSQ2 showed a greater propensity to form higher order polymeric structures than unphosphorylated CSQ2 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Stim1 plays a role in preventing heart failure following induced pressure overload or aging.
source: Stim1 is an ER/SR luminal Ca2+ sensor that regulates store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) and other Ca2+ sensing mechanisms in a variety of cell types (Soboloff et al., 2012; Bénard et al., 2016), including cardiomyocytes, where it plays a role in preventing heart failure following induced pressure overload or aging (Bénard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bénard et al., 2016.

claim: Stim1 has a conserved S-x-E site in the Ca2+-binding EF-hand region of the luminal portion.
source: We identified a conserved S-x-E site in the Ca2+-binding EF-hand region of the luminal portion of Stim1 (Figure 2A) (Stathopulos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A with sequence alignment.

claim: Stim1 was shown to be phosphorylated by Fam20C in cells and in vitro.
source: Stim1 was shown to be phosphorylated by Fam20C in cells and in vitro (Figure 2B and C) using the same techniques as above (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by autoradiography in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Stim1-Ser88Gly is a mutation recently discovered in a patient with heart disease.
source: In addition, Stim1-Ser88Gly (Figure 2A), a mutation recently discovered in a patient with heart disease (Harris et al., 2017) (see discussion), is less robustly phosphorylated than Stim1-WT in vitro and in cells (Figure 2C,D and E), suggesting that Fam20C phosphorylates Stim1-Ser88.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2017.

claim: Stim1-Ser88Gly is less robustly phosphorylated than Stim1-WT in vitro and in cells.
source: In addition, Stim1-Ser88Gly (Figure 2A), a mutation recently discovered in a patient with heart disease (Harris et al., 2017) (see discussion), is less robustly phosphorylated than Stim1-WT in vitro and in cells (Figure 2C,D and E), suggesting that Fam20C phosphorylates Stim1-Ser88.
evidence: This is demonstrated by autoradiography and densitometry in Figures 2C, D, and E.

claim: Fam20C phosphorylates Stim1-Ser88.
source: In addition, Stim1-Ser88Gly (Figure 2A), a mutation recently discovered in a patient with heart disease (Harris et al., 2017) (see discussion), is less robustly phosphorylated than Stim1-WT in vitro and in cells (Figure 2C,D and E), suggesting that Fam20C phosphorylates Stim1-Ser88.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced phosphorylation of the Ser88Gly mutant.

claim: Over-expression of WT Fam20C in cells caused significantly increased Stim1 activation under physiological Ca2+ levels in comparison to the catalytically inactive KI Fam20C.
source: We determined that over-expression of WT Fam20C in cells caused significantly increased Stim1 activation under physiological Ca2+ levels in comparison to the catalytically inactive KI Fam20C (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ca2+ handling proteins in the ER/SR by Fam20C is likely playing an important and complex regulatory role.
source: Taken together, phosphorylation of Ca2+ handling proteins in the ER/SR by Fam20C is likely playing an important and complex regulatory role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical data presented.

claim: A decrease in the peak amplitude of Ca2+ transients was observed for 9 months old Fam20C deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to controls.
source: A decrease in the peak amplitude (Figure 3C), corresponding to the extent of SR Ca2+ release, and an increase in the relaxation constant tau (Figure 3C), corresponding to the time it takes for SR Ca2+ reuptake, was observed for the Ca2+ transients of 9 months old Fam20C deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: An increase in the relaxation constant tau was observed for the Ca2+ transients of 9 months old Fam20C deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to controls.
source: A decrease in the peak amplitude (Figure 3C), corresponding to the extent of SR Ca2+ release, and an increase in the relaxation constant tau (Figure 3C), corresponding to the time it takes for SR Ca2+ reuptake, was observed for the Ca2+ transients of 9 months old Fam20C deficient cardiomyocytes in comparison to controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Similar results were obtained for the cell shortening measurements in 9 months old Fam20C deficient cardiomyocytes.
source: Similar results were obtained for the cell shortening measurements (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sarcomere length measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mildly reduced cardiomyocyte function was observed at baseline (2 months old) in Fam20C cKO mice.
source: We note mildly reduced cardiomyocyte function at baseline.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Following aging-induced stress, severe cardiomyocyte defects were identified from Fam20C deficiency, particularly in cardiomyocyte relaxation.
source: Strikingly, following aging-induced stress we identified severe cardiomyocyte defects from Fam20C deficiency, particularly in cardiomyocyte relaxation, which is likely causative of aging-induced diastolic heart failure (see below).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ca2+ transient and cell shortening measurements in Figure 3.

claim: Severe cardiomyocyte relaxation defects in Fam20C cKO mice are likely causative of aging-induced diastolic heart failure.
source: Strikingly, following aging-induced stress we identified severe cardiomyocyte defects from Fam20C deficiency, particularly in cardiomyocyte relaxation, which is likely causative of aging-induced diastolic heart failure (see below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relaxation defects and subsequent heart failure phenotype.

claim: Fam20C is an important regulator of SR Ca2+ cycling in stressed cardiomyocytes.
source: These results establish Fam20C as an important regulator of SR Ca2+cycling in stressed cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cardiomyocyte Ca2+ handling data in Figure 3.

claim: At 2 months of age, mild but statistically significant defects of cardiac contractility (Max dP/dt) were observed in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT mice.
source: At 2 months of age, we observe mild but statistically significant defects of cardiac contractility (Max dP/dt) (Figure 4A) and relaxation (Min dP/dt) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT mice, but no differences to the heart rate and other hemodynamic parameters were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 2 months of age, mild but statistically significant defects of cardiac relaxation (Min dP/dt) were observed in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT mice.
source: At 2 months of age, we observe mild but statistically significant defects of cardiac contractility (Max dP/dt) (Figure 4A) and relaxation (Min dP/dt) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT mice, but no differences to the heart rate and other hemodynamic parameters were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No differences to the heart rate and other hemodynamic parameters were observed at 2 months of age in Fam20C cKO mice.
source: At 2 months of age, we observe mild but statistically significant defects of cardiac contractility (Max dP/dt) (Figure 4A) and relaxation (Min dP/dt) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT mice, but no differences to the heart rate and other hemodynamic parameters were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Upon 9 months of aging, relaxation was significantly blunted in Fam20C cKO mice.
source: Upon 9 months of aging, relaxation was significantly blunted in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The isovolumetric relaxation constant tau was dramatically higher in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice, demonstrating delayed cardiac relaxation.
source: The isovolumetric relaxation constant tau was dramatically higher (Figure 4B), demonstrating delayed cardiac relaxation, and indicating overall diastolic dysfunction for 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice, which is likely to cause heart failure (see below).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice have overall diastolic dysfunction, which is likely to cause heart failure.
source: The isovolumetric relaxation constant tau was dramatically higher (Figure 4B), demonstrating delayed cardiac relaxation, and indicating overall diastolic dysfunction for 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice, which is likely to cause heart failure (see below).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diastolic dysfunction and established knowledge linking diastolic dysfunction to heart failure.

claim: Fam20C's role in contractility and relaxation is independent of acute β-adrenergic signaling in 2 months old mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that Fam20C's role in contractility and relaxation is independent of acute β-adrenergic signaling in 2 months old mice, via infusion of either dobutamine or esmolol (Schmid et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by hemodynamic measurements with dobutamine and esmolol infusion shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two and six months old Fam20C cKO mice were indistinguishable from their WT littermates by echocardiography.
source: Two and six months old Fam20C cKO mice were indistinguishable from their WT littermates.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Following 9 months of aging, Fam20C cKO mice displayed a decided increase in LV chamber size in both diastole and systole.
source: However, following 9 months of aging, Fam20C cKO mice displayed a decided increase in LV chamber size in both diastole and systole (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by echocardiographic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LV systolic function, as measured by fractional shortening (% FS), was dramatically decreased in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice.
source: LV systolic function, as measured by fractional shortening (% FS), was dramatically decreased in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 5A), suggesting that these mice were developing heart failure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by echocardiographic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice were developing heart failure.
source: LV systolic function, as measured by fractional shortening (% FS), was dramatically decreased in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 5A), suggesting that these mice were developing heart failure.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased fractional shortening, a marker of heart failure.

claim: Depressed systolic function was accompanied by a thinning of the LV walls in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice.
source: Depressed systolic function was accompanied by a thinning of the LV walls (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by echocardiographic measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice showed significant increases in the re-expression of fetal gene markers of cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, including ANP, BNP, and β-MHC.
source: Furthermore, measurement by qRT-PCR on 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice showed significant increases in the re-expression of fetal gene markers of cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, including atrial natriuretic factor (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), and β-myosin heavy chain (β-MHC), in comparison to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Gross morphological analysis showed enlarged hearts in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice, consistent with the development of DCM following 9 months of aging.
source: Gross morphological analysis showed enlarged hearts (Figure 6A), consistent with the development of DCM following 9 months of aging.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with macroscopic images of hearts.

claim: The observed heart failure in the Fam20C cKO mice following aging is likely due to dramatic SR Ca2+ handling defects and delayed cardiac relaxation.
source: The observed heart failure in the Fam20C cKO mice following aging is likely due to dramatic SR Ca2+ handling defects and delayed cardiac relaxation (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the cellular defects to the in vivo phenotype.

claim: In 2 months old Fam20C WT or cKO mice, no histological abnormalities or differences were identified.
source: In 2 months old Fam20C WT or cKO mice, no abnormalities or differences were identified.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Following 9 months of aging in the Fam20C cKO mice, H&E stained cardiac sections demonstrated ventricular dilation.
source: However, following 9 months of aging in the Fam20C cKO mice, Hematoxylin-Eosin (H and E) stained cardiac sections demonstrated ventricular dilation (Figure 6B), consistent with the echocardiographic analysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with H&E stained sections.

claim: Interstitial fibrosis was greatly increased in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice, while WT mice demonstrated no signs of fibrosis.
source: Using Masson's Trichrome staining, we established that interstitial fibrosis was greatly increased in Fam20C cKO mice, while WT mice demonstrated no signs of fibrosis following 9 months of aging (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C with Masson's Trichrome stained sections.

claim: The heart weight to body weight ratio was greater in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice.
source: Gravimetric analysis showed that the heart weight to body weight ratio was greater in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D with gravimetric measurements.

claim: TUNEL staining demonstrated significantly more apoptotic nuclei in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice.
source: Terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase-mediated dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) staining demonstrated significantly more apoptotic nuclei in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with TUNEL staining.

claim: The amount of cleaved PARP was increased in 9 months old Fam20C cKO heart lysates.
source: The amount of cleaved poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), a marker of apoptosis, was increased in Fam20C cKO heart lysates as determined by immunoblotting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with immunoblotting.

claim: Profibrotic gene expression markers (α-SMA, Coll-1a1, Coll-3a1, and CTGF) were increased in 9 months old Fam20C cKO mice.
source: Finally, profibrotic gene expression markers: α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), procollagen types I α1 (Coll-1a1) and III α1 (Coll-3a1), and connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) were increased in Fam20C cKO mice upon aging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C with qRT-PCR measurements.

claim: The response to pressure overload for 4 weeks was similar between genotypes of 2 months old Fam20C WT and cKO mice.
source: The response to pressure overload for 4 weeks was similar between genotypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) of 2 months old Fam20C WT and cKO mice, both of which developed LV wall thickening (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C with echocardiographic measurements.

claim: Both Fam20C WT and cKO mice developed LV wall thickening following 4 weeks of TAC.
source: The response to pressure overload for 4 weeks was similar between genotypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) of 2 months old Fam20C WT and cKO mice, both of which developed LV wall thickening (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C with echocardiographic measurements.

claim: Fam20C cKO mice developed significantly exaggerated LV chamber dilation following 4 weeks of TAC in comparison to their WT littermates.
source: However, Fam20C cKO mice developed significantly exaggerated LV chamber dilation (Figure 7A) and showed further deterioration in cardiac function (Figure 7A) in comparison to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with echocardiographic measurements.

claim: Fam20C cKO mice showed further deterioration in cardiac function following 4 weeks of TAC in comparison to their WT littermates.
source: However, Fam20C cKO mice developed significantly exaggerated LV chamber dilation (Figure 7A) and showed further deterioration in cardiac function (Figure 7A) in comparison to their WT littermates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with echocardiographic measurements.

claim: The heart weight to body weight ratio was higher in Fam20C cKO mice following TAC.
source: Gravimetric analysis of isolated hearts showed that the heart weight to body weight ratio was higher in Fam20C cKO mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with gravimetric measurements.

claim: Re-expression of cardiac fetal genes further confirmed the presence of exaggerated heart failure in Fam20C cKO mice following TAC in comparison to WT littermates.
source: Re-expression of cardiac fetal genes (Figure 7B) further confirmed the presence of exaggerated heart failure in Fam20C cKO mice in comparison to WT littermates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with qRT-PCR measurements.

claim: Fam20C cKO mice heart sections showed increased fibrosis following TAC.
source: We determined also that Fam20C cKO mice heart sections showed increased fibrosis (Figure 7C) and apoptosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E) following TAC.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with Masson's Trichrome staining.

claim: Fam20C cKO mice heart sections showed increased apoptosis following TAC.
source: We determined also that Fam20C cKO mice heart sections showed increased fibrosis (Figure 7C) and apoptosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E) following TAC.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E with TUNEL staining.

claim: After 2 weeks of chronic isoproterenol infusion, Fam20C cKO mice showed a significantly increased heart weight to body weight ratio.
